Planning services

Wedding planning, from the first decision to the last week

How to plan a wedding in Australia without carrying every part of it yourself. The month by month timeline, what belongs on the checklist, the points where couples reliably stall, and what help is worth buying at each stage.

Where do you actually start when you plan a wedding?

Most guides on how to plan a wedding open with a checklist. Start with four numbers instead, in this order: the budget ceiling, the guest count, how flexible the date is, and the kind of venue you want. Everything else is downstream of those four, and most later problems come from settling them in the wrong order, or not at all.

Guest count is the one people avoid, and the most expensive thing on the list. Every guest carries catering, drinks, a chair, a place setting and a share of the floor space. Moving from 90 to 120 guests can push you out of the venue entirely, so settle the number before you book the room.

Date flexibility is the cheapest lever you have. Peak season in most of Australia is spring, roughly September to November, and autumn, roughly March to May, and Saturdays in those months are priced highest and booked first. If your date is fixed, you are shopping in a smaller market, so start earlier.

Only then does the venue search make sense, because a venue quoted for the wrong guest number is not information. This is where some couples buy venue sourcing on its own.

The order matters more than the speed

Couples who book a venue before settling the guest count end up trimming the list to fit the room or paying to expand the room to fit the list. Write the number down and treat it as a decision rather than an estimate.

Who is paying, and for what

If parents or family are contributing, agree what the contribution covers before you spend any of it. An unspoken assumption about who pays for the bar is the most common source of tension in an Australian wedding budget.

Timeline

What does a wedding planning timeline look like month by month?

The Australian shape of it, on a nine to fourteen month engagement. Compress it if your date is closer, but keep the order.

A month by month wedding planning timeline. Shorter engagements compress the middle rather than the ends.
WhenWhat to lock inWhy it has to happen now
Twelve to fourteen monthsBudget ceiling, guest count, date flexibility, venue shortlist and site visits. Book the venue.Peak Saturdays go first, and every other supplier needs your date and venue before they can quote.
Ten to twelve monthsPhotographer, celebrant and the wedding party. Start the catering conversation if the venue does not supply it.These book out furthest ahead and none can be duplicated on the day.
Eight to ten monthsMusic, florist, cake, hire and styling direction. Accommodation blocks if guests are travelling.Peak season suppliers are choosing between enquiries by now.
Six to eight monthsOutfits ordered, invitations designed, transport booked, wet weather plan agreed in writing.Outfits need fitting time, and a wet weather plan invented in the final week is not a plan.
Four to six monthsMenu and drinks confirmed, ceremony detail agreed, invitations sent.Australian couples typically send invitations three to four months out, and catering needs those numbers.
Three monthsRSVP tracking, dietary requirements, trials, first draft of the run sheet.The last comfortable moment to change anything structural.
Six to eight weeksFinal guest numbers, seating chart, rehearsal booked, and the handover if you are using a coordinator.Most venues want final numbers here and charge on them whoever turns up.
Four weeksEvery supplier confirmed in writing with arrival times and access details.A booking not confirmed at four weeks is the thing that goes wrong at four days.
Two weeksRun sheet circulated to every supplier and the venue. Contingencies agreed.Suppliers build their own week around your run sheet. Late is the same as missing.
The week ofDeliveries sequenced, bump in confirmed, personal items packed, one decision maker nominated.Somebody has to be reachable and authorised, and it should not be you.

Scroll the table sideways to see every column.

A shorter engagement is not a problem in itself. What fails is running the same list out of order. If you have six months, do the twelve month row first and compress the middle.

The checklist

What should a wedding planning checklist actually contain?

Most published checklists are lists of purchases. A wedding planning checklist worth keeping tracks five things, and only one is shopping.

Money, tracked against a ceiling

One document with every quote, deposit, balance and due date, measured against the number you agreed at the start, plus a contingency line. Easy Weddings put the average Australian wedding budget at $35,315 in its 2025 Wedding Industry Report, which is a reference point, not a target.

Paper, and what it commits you to

Every contract, with the deposit, balance date, cancellation terms and postponement clause noted. Most couples read the price and skip the terms. The terms matter when something changes.

People, and who has told you what

RSVPs, dietary requirements, accessibility needs, who is travelling and who has a job on the day. The section that grows fastest in the final two months.

Logistics, in time order

Access times, bump in windows, deliveries, transport and who returns the hire. Ordinary items live here too: the marriage paperwork, the rings and the box everything goes home in.

The day itself, in one document

The run sheet. Not a schedule of your day, a schedule of everyone's day, including suppliers you will never see. If your wedding planning checklist produces nothing else, it should produce this.

On-the-day coordination

The hours

How much time does planning a wedding actually take?

More than people budget for, and not evenly spread. Worth being honest about before you decide whether to buy help.

Airtasker's Australian cost guide, updated February 2025, estimates that planning a single wedding takes 200 to 300 hours. Across a twelve month engagement that is four to six hours a week for a year, and it is not spread evenly. The load concentrates in the first two months and in the last two, when confirmation and admin arrive at once.

Most of those hours are not creative. They are chasing: a supplier who has not replied in nine days, a quote that changed, whether the florist and the stylist have the same access time, and the same three questions from four family members. That is the work wedding planning services remove.

If you are both working full time and the wedding is in peak season, be realistic about which four hours a week those are. The usual reason a couple buys wedding planning help at short notice is not that they cannot plan. It is that the hours were never there.

The sticking points

Where do couples get stuck?

Four places, and they are the same four every time.

01

The dead middle

Months five to eight, when the exciting bookings are done and what remains is admin. Nothing gets decided for six weeks and the backlog lands when it is most expensive to fix. Book a standing hour each week.

02

The guest list

It is never really about the number. It is a family expectation nobody has said out loud. Settle it early, in one conversation, and write down the answer.

03

The budget that moves

Every wedding grows. The problem is not growth, it is untracked growth. If you cannot see the total in one place, you find out in month ten that it moved in month four.

What a planner costs
04

The final six weeks

Confirmation, final numbers, seating, payments and a run sheet arrive at once, usually while you are working. The stretch people most often hand over.

On-the-day coordination

Getting help

What does wedding planning help look like at each stage?

Wedding planning services are sold in levels, and the one that suits you depends on where you are standing when you ask.

01

Nothing booked yet

Full planning. The planner starts at the brief, finds the venue, books every supplier and holds the budget. Engaged nine to fourteen months out.

02

Venue booked, little else

Partial planning. The planner picks up the suppliers you have not chosen and takes the jobs that keep sliding. Four to eight months out.

03

Most of it booked, no run sheet

On-the-day coordination. Your plan stays as it is and someone else confirms and runs it. Handover four to six weeks before.

04

Only the venue is missing

Venue sourcing on its own. A planner writes the brief, shortlists against it and reviews the contract, without taking on the rest.

Buying wedding planning services is not all or nothing. If you know which level you want, go straight to wedding planners to find the person. If not, the planning services comparison sets the levels side by side.

Straight answers

Wedding planning questions

How long does it take to plan a wedding in Australia?

Nine to fourteen months is the usual window for a full plan, and Airtasker's Australian guide, updated February 2025, estimates 200 to 300 hours of work inside it. Shorter is possible. What shrinks is choice, particularly for peak Saturdays in spring and autumn.

What is the first thing to do when planning a wedding?

Settle four numbers before you look at a venue: the budget ceiling, the guest count, how flexible the date is and the type of venue you want. Guest count is the expensive one, because it decides catering, drinks, floor space and which venues are possible at all.

Do I need a planner or just a wedding planning checklist?

A checklist tells you what to do. It does not do it, chase it or absorb the hours. If you have the time, a good wedding planning checklist and a shared budget document carry you a long way. Where couples reliably buy wedding planning services is the final six weeks, which is why on-the-day coordination is the most commonly bought planning product here.

Can I plan a wedding in six months?

Yes, and plenty of Australian couples do. Run the same order, not the same pace: settle the four numbers in week one, book the venue immediately, then photographer and celebrant. Expect fewer options on peak Saturdays, and be flexible on the day of the week.

What does a wedding planner charge in Australia?

Easy Weddings, in a guide updated February 2026, puts full-service planning at $5,000 to $6,000, a day-of coordinator at roughly $1,500 to $2,000 and hourly consultations at $75 to $100. Airtasker's Australian guide gives $1,000 to $20,000 with a median near $8,000 and a common 10 to 15 per cent of budget model. The variable is scope.
